intro.opening: A private, family-paced run at Egypt's classic itinerary: Cairo, a Nile cruise from Luxor to Aswan, and Cairo again. What families need is not a simplified Egypt but a paced one, with a structure that alternates intensity with recovery and gives children something to do with their hands as well as their eyes.
intro.whyRoute: The journey moves through three registers: Cairo and the Giza plateau to open, a Nile cruise from Luxor south to Aswan, and a return to Cairo to close. The cruise is the spine. It moves you between Luxor, Edfu, Kom Ombo and Aswan without repacking a suitcase each night, and its onboard downtime (pool, cooking class, hieroglyphics workshop) makes the shore days sustainable for children. Sailing from Luxor to Aswan, you travel upstream against the current and meet the temples roughly in the order their builders understood: the state religion of Thebes first, then the older sites further south, arriving at Aswan, the edge of the ancient Egyptian world, at the end.
intro.closingLine: Nine days is not enough to exhaust Egypt. Done this way, it is enough to give a family a version of the country they will not need to correct later.

stayAndTravel.hotels: A hotel in Cairo on the first night.
stayAndTravel.river: A Nile cruise ship from Luxor south to Aswan, by way of Edfu and Kom Ombo, with a pool, a hieroglyphics workshop and a cooking class on board.
stayAndTravel.flight: A domestic flight from Cairo to Luxor at the start of the river journey, and one from Aswan back to Cairo at the end.
stayAndTravel.everyDay: A licensed English-speaking Egyptologist guide, private air-conditioned transfers and bottled water. The trip is private, operated for your party alone and never shared with a group, and it scales to any party size.

want the classic Cairo-and-cruise shape, paced for a party that includes children

intro.makeItYoursIntro: A private journey is built around your party, not the other way around. Common changes:

days.title: Arrival, the Giza plateau, the Grand Egyptian Museum and the Sound and Light Show

segments.label: morning
segments.heading: Giza
segments.text: You're met at Cairo International Airport and transferred to your hotel, and the first day moves straight to its main business: the Giza plateau. The three pyramids of Khufu, Khafre and Menkaure stand above the desert beside the Great Sphinx. Built around 2500 BC, they are not the oldest monuments in Egypt, but they set the terms of every visit.

segments.label: afternoon
segments.text: The Grand Egyptian Museum, at the edge of the Giza plateau and a short hop from the pyramids, opened fully on 1 November 2025. It holds the complete Tutankhamun collection, displayed together for the first time: the gold mask, the nested shrines and the objects packed into his tomb. The original Egyptian Museum on Tahrir Square can be substituted or combined on request.

segments.label: evening
segments.text: As the light goes, the Sound and Light Show at the pyramids closes the day: the plateau narrated against floodlit stone. It is theatrical, and younger travellers tend to find it memorable.

sites: Sound and Light Show at the pyramids
days.travel: Meet at Cairo International Airport, private transfer to your hotel

days.title: Flight to Luxor and boarding the Nile cruise
body: A domestic flight takes you to Luxor, the site of ancient Thebes and religious capital of the New Kingdom empire, and you transfer to the Nile cruise ship that will be your home on the river. The first afternoon is given over to the ship: the pool, cultural programmes and the Nile passing the windows, a useful decompression after the density of Cairo. Dinner is on board as the ship begins south.
days.travel: Domestic flight Cairo → Luxor · private transfer to the cruise ship
days.pace: An afternoon on board after the density of Cairo

days.title: The West Bank: the Valley of the Kings, Hatshepsut and the Colossi of Memnon

segments.label: morning
segments.heading: The West Bank
segments.text: The West Bank is the side the ancient Egyptians dedicated to the dead. In the Valley of the Kings, New Kingdom pharaohs were buried from the sixteenth century BC onward, in tombs whose corridors and chambers are still painted with scenes of the journey through the underworld. More than sixty have been found; several are open on any given day, and the guides direct the family to the most significant and accessible. Then the Mortuary Temple of Hatshepsut at Deir el-Bahari, rising in three colonnaded terraces against the cliff, and the Colossi of Memnon, two seated figures of Amenhotep III.

segments.label: afternoon
segments.text: Back on the ship, children can take part in a hieroglyphics workshop, learning the basic system of ancient Egyptian writing and producing their own inscribed messages, while adults use the ship's amenities. The evening is on the river.

days.travel: Private transfers to the West Bank and back to the ship

days.title: The East Bank: Karnak, Luxor Temple and the Avenue of Sphinxes
body: The second Luxor day stays on the East Bank, the living side. Karnak is a temple precinct built and rebuilt by successive pharaohs over roughly 1,500 years. Its Great Hypostyle Hall holds 134 columns, the tallest 21 metres high, and this day leaves time to walk it without urgency. Luxor Temple follows, with the Avenue of Sphinxes that once connected it to Karnak, a processional road some three kilometres long and now walkable for much of its length. The guides use both sites to explain how the state religion worked: the processions, the festivals and the inner sanctuaries only priests could enter. In the afternoon the ship sails on toward Edfu.
days.travel: Private transfers · afternoon sailing toward Edfu
days.pace: Time to walk Karnak without urgency

days.title: The Temple of Horus at Edfu and a cooking class on board
body: The Temple of Horus at Edfu is the best-preserved temple in Egypt. Its walls, roof and inner sanctuary survive, so standing inside shows how an Egyptian temple worked as a building: how light was controlled and how the spaces contracted toward the sanctuary. It was built between 237 and 57 BC, but in a rigorously traditional form, which makes it a key for reading the older temples you have already seen. The afternoon sails on to Kom Ombo, and in the evening there's an Egyptian cooking class on board: traditional dishes taught and then eaten.
days.travel: By cruise, Edfu to Kom Ombo

days.title: The Temple of Kom Ombo and the Crocodile Museum
body: Kom Ombo sits above the east bank where the river bends. Its temple was dedicated to two gods at once, Sobek the crocodile deity and Horus the Elder, and its whole plan is doubled: two parallel axes run side by side through identical halls and sanctuaries, in an exact symmetry that is slightly uncanny once you notice it. Next to the temple, the crocodile museum holds mummified crocodiles from a nearby necropolis, and it tends to be what younger travellers remember most. In the afternoon the ship continues south toward Aswan.
days.travel: By cruise, Kom Ombo to Aswan

days.title: Philae, a felucca around Elephantine Island and Nubian music

segments.label: morning
segments.heading: Philae
segments.text: Aswan is Egypt's southernmost significant city, set where the Nile narrows toward the first cataract, smaller and slower than Cairo and Luxor. The day begins at the Temple of Isis on Philae Island, reached by motorboat. The temple was reassembled here in the 1970s to save it from the rising waters of Lake Nasser, in the same UNESCO rescue that lifted Abu Simbel, and the worship of Isis continued here into the fifth century AD.

segments.label: afternoon
segments.text: A felucca, the traditional white-sailed Nile boat, takes you around Elephantine Island at the wind's pace, past the corniche and the botanical gardens of Kitchener's Island. The contrast with the temple mornings is the point.

segments.label: evening
segments.text: The day closes with a Nubian music and dance session, an introduction to the Nubian people, whose homeland was flooded by Lake Nasser and who rebuilt their communities on the banks around Aswan. Children tend to find the participatory rhythms more engaging than any temple explanation.

days.travel: Motorboat to Philae · felucca around Elephantine Island

days.title: Flight to Cairo, Khan el-Khalili and a farewell Nile dinner cruise

segments.label: morning
segments.text: Disembarkation, and a flight north to Cairo.

segments.label: afternoon
segments.text: Khan el-Khalili, the medieval bazaar quarter of Islamic Cairo, trading continuously since the fourteenth century: dense, noisy, negotiable and very good for souvenirs, from brass and copper work and spices sold by weight from open sacks to cotton, papyrus and jewellery. The guides know which parts of the market are worth the time and which are not.

segments.label: evening
segments.text: A farewell Nile dinner cruise closes the trip, with the lit city on both banks and minarets and bridges moving past as the boat turns: a formal close to a journey that began with the Nile in a different mood, at a different latitude.

days.travel: Domestic flight Aswan → Cairo · private transfers

days.title: Departure
body: A transfer to the airport. For families with a later departure, the guides can suggest options.

options: Combine the Grand Egyptian Museum with the Tahrir Egyptian Museum, or substitute the Tahrir museum
